finding: On pixltagger's own labels a frozen-DINOv3 logistic probe put 56 to 74 true positives in its top 100 for malformed hand, foot and bad anatomy (chance would give 6 to 20), but every fit used about 1,200 or more labelled pictures, DINOv3 rather than PixlStash's CLIP vectors, and was never compared with the near-neighbour vote, so it cannot answer the 50-200-verdict question in #2678.
wouldSettle: The held-out learning curve of notebook idea 4: on PixlStash's stored CLIP ViT-B/32 embeddings, for the tags with the most confirm/reject verdicts, fit the logistic regression on 50, 100 and 200 random verdicts, run the near-neighbour vote from the same verdicts, and compare the share of confirmed pictures among each method's top-ranked held-out pictures over several random draws.

followUps.title: Shrink the already-saved DINOv3 probe to 50, 100 and 200 labels
followUps.body: pixltagger already keeps DINOv3 picture features and labels for its 1,707-picture evaluation set on disk, and this round showed that a simple classifier fitted on about 1,365 of those labels ranks anomaly tags well. Nobody knows how much of that survives with the 50 to 200 labels a PixlStash user would actually give. Refit the same classifier on random draws of 50, 100 and 200 labels from those saved features, repeat each draw several times, and count how many true positives land in its top 100 of the remaining pictures. It needs no new picture processing. If the count holds up at 100 labels, that supports computing a stronger embedding in PixlStash (notebook idea 9); if it collapses, the label count rather than the embedding is the limit.

plain.idea: Teach the computer a picture label, such as 'malformed hand', by showing it examples a person has already marked yes or no, and let it fit a simple rule over a summary of each picture. Here the summary came from a strong image model and the examples came from a separate tagging project.
settles: Does the rule's list of best guesses contain far more real examples than a random pick?
Was it tried with a few hundred examples or fewer, as PixlStash users would give?
Was it tried on PixlStash's own picture summaries, against PixlStash's existing method?
plain.showed: Given about twelve hundred marked pictures, the rule's best guesses were mostly right for malformed hands, feet and general anatomy errors, far better than a random pick. But it was never tried with as few examples as PixlStash users would give, never on the picture summaries PixlStash keeps, and never against PixlStash's current method. So it does not yet say whether the feature would help.
